Arsenal’s interest is not limited to mere scouting, with reports indicating that the Premier League champions have already contacted his representatives, although no agreement or formal transfer bid has been confirmed. Barcelona have followed Fresneda since 2023 Fresneda is a familiar name to Barcelona’s sporting department. The Catalan club seriously considered signing him in the summer of 2023 , when he was still playing for Valladolid and regarded as one of Spain’s promising young full-backs. Barcelona ultimately chose to bring Joao Cancelo back to the club instead, while Fresneda moved to Sporting for a reported fee of around €9 million. His contract in Lisbon runs until June 2028. Barcelona are still keeping an eye on Ivan Fresneda. (Photo by Gualter Fatia/Getty Images) Interest from Barcelona has resurfaced in recent weeks , as reports from Portugal have indicated the Blaugrana are monitoring his progress, with sporting director Deco involved in assessing the defender. Simply put, Barcelona are looking for a long-term solution at right-back after considering other targets, including Pedro Porro. Sporting hold a strong position in the transfer battle Crucially, Fresneda’s improvement has also strengthened Sporting’s position, with the Portuguese club now keen to extend his contract until 2031 and retain an €80 million release clause, making a potential transfer difficult to negotiate. For Barcelona, Arsenal’s contact already poses a big problem, and if the player ultimately signs an extension with the Portuguese club, their pursuit could well and truly rest once and for all.

sports.description: From England: Roma tracking Federico Chiesa New confirmation is coming from England regarding the future of Federico Chiesa, one of the wingers linked to Roma ahead of the January transfer window. According to The Athletic , the 1997-born player will leave Liverpool in 2027, either during the winter transfer window or at the end of the season. The former Juventus player is now on the fringes of Andoni Iraola’s coaching project, having only played two minutes of the Premier League match against Manchester City on October 11th since the start of the season. As reported in recent days by Corriere dello Sport, Chiesa has been offered to Roma, with Tony D’Amico working to provide Gasperini with a new attacking winger. Inter, Atalanta, and Lazio are also reportedly interested in the 2021 European champion, while the player is reportedly keen on a return to Juventus. Complicating the former Juventus player’s potential arrival in the capital are Liverpool’s demands, which have so far valued the Italian at around €15 million, along with a salary of €7.5 million per season. Roma, on the other hand, are reportedly keen to strengthen their attack through a loan with an option to buy.

sports.title: De Zerbi: Sunderland loss in first game when his Tottenham 'was born’
sports.description: FILE PHOTO - Tottenham Hotspur manager Roberto De Zerbi reacts during the English Premier League soccer match between Tottenham Hotspur and Crystal Palace at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. De Zerbi saw his new side beaten 1-0 at the Stadium of Light in April, a loss which left the club in the relegation zone and sparked emotional scenes at full-time. The reaction of Tottenham’s devastated players helped determine De Zerbi’s approach during an ultimately successful final six matches of the 2025-26 campaign which saw survival clinched on the final day. Ahead of Sunday’s trip to Sunderland, De Zerbi said: “I am thinking of showing this video from the end of the game to the players. “I don’t want us to forget this moment. It is the key for my Tottenham. Maybe in the future with another coach this will change, but my Tottenham was born that day. “That day it was tough to accept the defeat, tough to accept the behaviour after the defeat, but it was the crucial day and I have a great memory of the behaviour even though we lost the game, because I understood better what we needed at the time. “We didn’t need football. We didn’t need so many principles on the pitch. We needed completely different things. “Too many people sad, many of them suffering too much, maybe too many people who didn’t believe enough in themselves, not enough smiles. Now we have a good atmosphere, but we can’t forget. “It’s just to remember, to keep inside of us and to believe in what we’re doing. Not just me and the players, but also the club together, because that situation changed. “Credit for the club, credit for the owner. sports.title: Winning is the only option for Iraola ahead of first Merseyside derby
sports.description: FILE PHOTO - Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola gestures on the touchline during the UEFA Champions League soccer match between Fenerbahce and Liverpool at Sukru Saracoglu Stadium. (is associated with: «Winning is the only option for Iraola ahead of first Merseyside derby») Adam Davy/PA Wire/dpa Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola heads into his first Merseyside derby knowing there is only one option: win. Just two defeats in the last 34 meetings with Everton mean expectations for the short trip to Hill Dickinson Stadium are high. Most of the statistics associated with England’s most-played derby favour the Reds, looking for a fourth successive victory over their neighbours for the first time since August 1991, as the Toffees have won just one of the last 15 home encounters against Liverpool. As a proud Basque, Iraola knows the significance of local rivalries, but Sunday’s game is on an all together higher level. “I played a lot, also a big derby – Athletic [Bilbao]-Real Sociedad. I think they are special because – the same as here – you have a lot of friends that are from the opposing team, sometimes a member of your family even,” he said. “Definitely it’s a game that lasts longer. It’s not a game you play and, OK, you speak a little bit next week. “No, normally this thing lasts long and the winner reminds the other side normally a lot of time. “I experienced it a lot as a player and this is going to be my first one here, but I can feel everyone wants to win it, yes.” Liverpool’s form is encouraging as they have won their last three in all competitions while Everton go into the game off the back of a 4-0 humbling by Brentford, their first defeat in four matches in all competitions. The two teams were separated by five places and five points heading into the weekend but Iraola will not allow his fourth-placed side to be complacent. “I think it is a derby and derbies are always different. It doesn’t matter where you are in the standings, it doesn’t matter the run that you are in,” he added. Four players – Jeremy Jacquet, Ronald Araujo, Bradley Barcola and Trey Nyoni – look set for their derby debuts. The 21-year-old Jacquet has slotted into the centre of defence to become Virgil van Dijk’s regular partner and has impressed but his composure will be tested in the derby, although Iraola does not believe the occasion will trouble him. “He has this self-confidence. He is also improving with the language and that always helps with communications with team-mates,” he said of the newly capped France international. “He doesn’t have a lot of games or experience, but he is in high-level games and playing with the national team. “Also, he has help from experienced players around him. That helps when you are young, but he is giving back with performances.”

sports.title: Baylor Set to Name Multi-Time Conference Champion as Next Head Coach
sports.description: DALLAS, TEXAS - DECEMBER 26: Head coach Jeff Traylor of the UTSA Roadrunners reacts during the second quarter F in the 2025 SERVPRO First Responder Bowl at Gerald J. Ford Stadium on December 26, 2025 in Dallas, Texas. (Photo by Sam Hodde/Getty Images) Getty One of the open Power Four coaching jobs is set to be filled, at least that’s according to ESPN’s Pete Thamel as of Friday night. According to Thamel, Baylor is going to hire UTSA head coach Jeff Traylor as the school’s next leader. Baylor Set to Hire UTSA’s Jeff Traylor as Their Next Head Coach With an official announcement expected to take place in the coming days, Traylor will stay in Texas and jump up the Big 12 after posting a 63-28 record in seven seasons with the Roadrunners. He has UTSA at 10-2 and about to play for a conference title in the American Championship Game. Another win and Traylor, 58, would have his highest victory total since 2022, back when his team finished 11-3 after a loss in the Cure Bowl. But no matter how 2026 ends, Traylor has proven to be a consistent winner at the Group of 5 level. Traylor Turned UTSA Into a Championship Program In seven seasons, he owns a career winning clip of .689, has capped off every season with a bowl appearance, has three-straight bowl wins and two conference championships (both when a member of Conference USA). Before joining UTSA ahead of the 2020 campaign, Traylor served as Arkansas’ assistant head coach and running backs coach in 2018 and 2019. He served in the same position at SMU in 2017 and was a social teams coach at the University of Texas in 2015 and 2016. Traylor started his coaching career working up the Texas high school ranks in the late 1990s, eventually landing a head role at Gilmer High School from 2000-2014. And while Traylor may not be a flashy name nationally, he will now be able to test his system and recruiting chops with resources at his disposal. Baylor is Hoping for More Consistent Success Moving Forward Baylor is looking to turn the page to a more successful next chapter after firing Dave Aranda in late October. Aranda was 40-40 overall and 26-32 in conference play in six seasons. Never able to duplicate his second year, when he led the Bears to a 12-2 record, a Big 12 title and a victory in the Sugar Bowl, Aranda was 4-3 in 2026 at the time of his dismissal, a disappointing start to a season that followed going 5-7 in 2025. Aranda only reached a bowl game in three seasons, losing his most recent opportunities in 2022 and 2024. sports.description: Steven Gerrard: Florian Wirtz has his confidence back and can shine at Liverpool Steven Gerrard believes Florian Wirtz has got his confidence back at Liverpool and said the midfielder will be fine after a difficult start at Anfield. Wirtz has found form in recent weeks and has six goals and two assists in his last five appearances for club and country. The Germany international has scored in each of his last three appearances for Liverpool, a welcome upturn after a tough first season with the club. Wirtz is already closing in on his goal contribution numbers in the Premier League from last season, after a first campaign that saw the 23-year-old struggle to impact games. The midfielder faced scrutiny amid a £116m transfer fee from Bayer Leverkusen, but is now beginning to show his best form in a Liverpool shirt. Former Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard believes Wirtz now has the tools around him to thrive, and said the signing of Bradley Barcola has helped his game. "I've watched this kid closely since the moment he arrived. I felt like, when he arrived, you could sort of see the heavy transfer fee on his shoulders," Gerrard told the BBC. ‘A dream situation’: Gerrard explains why Wirtz is finally thriving at Liverpool "[After] A bit of criticism, you could see him playing with a little bit of a lack of belief, a little bit of [a lack of] confidence. I felt that Wirtz was playing in this Liverpool team and he didn't really have the tools he needs to be effective. "Now he's got them. Especially with [Bradley] Barcola as well. So, it's a dream situation for Wirtz now. His confidence is back, his shoulders are back. He's enjoying his football. Internationally it's working. It's working at his club. If we can keep all of the fit talent around him, he's going to be fine."

The German club will only entertain a January departure if a suitor tables an 'astronomical offer', defined as a bid surpassing the €100m (£83.5m) threshold. Leipzig's reluctance stems from their own ambitions this season. Sitting fourth in the Bundesliga and still battling for a play-off spot in the Champions League league phase, the club want to retain their strongest squad for the remainder of the term. Nusa's rapid rise in Germany Nusa has justified that lofty valuation with a sensational campaign in Germany. Having arrived at Leipzig from Club Brugge two years ago in a €21m (£17.8m) deal, the forward has become one of the team's standout performers, registering nine goals and eight assists in 17 appearances so far this season. His form at club level mirrors his growing influence on the international stage. Nusa has already cemented his place as a key figure in Norway's attack, netting ten goals in 36 appearances for his country. What's next for Arsenal? Arsenal now face a decisive call ahead of the January window: test RB Leipzig's resolve with a massive bid or explore alternative attacking targets for Arteta. Leipzig have already proven they are willing to play the long game in the transfer market. Earlier this year, the Bundesliga outfit resisted selling Yan Diomande in January before agreeing a deal worth up to £120m with Real Madrid in the summer. Unless Arsenal are prepared to meet Leipzig's steep winter demands, they may have to wait until the end of the season to make another move for Nusa.

technology.title: Quantum: 'Five years, that's all we got…'
technology.description: SC26 in Chicago had the usual quantum booths, discussions, and hallway optimism. A lot of people were talking about integration with classical HPC and Slurm scheduling for quantum processors, co-design platforms, and GPU-accelerated error correction tools. That part is real and useful. What was harder to find was any result that changed the basic math on when quantum systems will actually do something a supercomputer can't already handle better. I had a long conversation in St. Louis (SC25) with a contact who works deep in quantum and has spent decades in HPC. He's not a skeptic for sport, although that can be fun, sure. Over a grifted free dinner in Chicago (the best kind), his take this year remains the same: the hype keeps outrunning the error rates. Quantum computers generate too many errors to give usable answers on anything interesting. Fixing that is the whole game. And that's a five-year game, minimum. Much like the Bowie anthem in the title. Qubits by the numbers There are two kinds of qubits. Physical qubits are the actual hardware: ions, superconducting circuits, and atoms in a trap. Logical qubits are the ones that do the computation. Each logical qubit is built out of many physical ones so the system can detect and correct errors while it runs. With the traditional surface-code approach, one logical qubit often needs somewhere between 500 and 2,000 physical qubits backing it up, depending on the hardware and the code. One logical qubit by itself is useless. Estimates for basic scientific modeling and small-scale simulation sit in the 100-to-500 logical-qubit range. Take the midpoint of 300. At the low end of the overhead that is 150,000 physical qubits. At the high end it is several million. That is only for early science. Commercial work like molecular mapping for pharma, large optimization problems, complex financial models, pushes into the thousands of logical qubits. National-security and encryption-related work sits even higher. Those numbers have not magically shrunk. A system that can map a modestly sized drug molecule, or run a materials simulation that is still too slow on classical machines, is the kind of workload people actually mean when they talk about useful quantum advantage. Until the logical-qubit counts get there with error rates low enough to finish the job, those problems stay on the machines we already know how to build. Ok, so let's just scale it up This is the world of HPC, we know how to scale stuff, right? Yes, but this isn't a matter of adding a few more racks. Scaling to an additional few hundred thousand physical qubits is not a rack or two or ten. It's probably a dedicated building with its own cryogenics, control electronics, and power draw that is still measured in megawatts even before you get useful logical capacity. technology.title: Unkernel and Trynix just transported computing to 2035
technology.description: What's the difference between just-for-fun demo hacks, and serious carefully designed large-scale software architecture? It's the quick-and-dirty jobs that end up transforming computing. A blog post earlier this week called 2035 came early led the Reg FOSS desk down what we thought was a fascinating, and possibly quite scary, rabbit-hole… but it turned out to be an entire warren. We thought we were still in 2026, but in turns out that in some ways, tech just leaped forward a decade. To try to convey the point of this blog post – why what had been just a fun clever little hack has the potential to take half a century of OS and hypervisor design and throw it out of the nearest window – will take quite a lot of unpacking. If you bear with us, we will try to walk you through it. To get started, we need to go back a decade or more. Stick with this: there are laughs, as well as hammers taken to beloved ideas. The year of 2035 and the ideas around that come from a remarkable talk by Gary Bernhardt of Destroy All Software, which is both funny and highly educational. It will really massively assist understanding what this article and the technology is all about if you have the time to watch the talks. The Reg FOSS desk is not at all fond of spoken-word video as a medium – we much prefer to read than listen – but the three talks we're going to mention are golden, among the very best presentations this century in all of computing and IT. Seriously, they are worth your time. As a preface, before we go into Bernhardt's half-hour information-dense talk, let's warm up with a four-minute funny one. But first, let's look at the context for that. Step 0: JavaScript is the language of web programming In 2009, Jeff Atwood laid this out in an article called All Programming is Web Programming . It's still coming true today. Software is getting very blurred around the edges. The entire SaaS industry means that massive organizations run on web apps. Tech like Electron embeds a web browser inside JavaScript apps built in Node.js, while Progressive Web Apps make websites look like local program windows. The most popular desktop Linux in the world is ChromeOS Flex, which doesn't support local native applications at all. Everything is browser windows, even the desktop. It's all built in JavaScript. And yet… Step 1: JavaScript is kind of weird and kind of bad. Bernhardt made this case in 2012, with a celebrated lightning talk called Wat , from the CodeMash conference in 2012. Wat walks through a whole list of examples of how JavaScript is a very strange programming language and does very strange things that are not at all what you might expect. Some of the jokes will make more sense to programmers, but we reckon anyone who has ever fought with a recalcitrant bit of software will get some laughs from it – and that probably applies to all readers of The Register. Step 2: JavaScript is in the process of conquering the world. Bernhardt moved on to much bigger ideas at PyCon 2014

technology.title: Smartphone shipments face another bleak year before modest 2028 comeback
technology.description: Global smartphone shipments are forecast to fall 14 percent this year and another 6 percent in 2027, with a recovery not expected until 2028. That's the outlook from Counterpoint Research's latest Smartphone Market Outlook Tracker , which points to rising memory costs and constrained supplies as continuing pressure on handset makers and buyers. The downturn was particularly sharp in the third quarter: IDC and Omdia estimated year-on-year shipment declines of 22 percent and 20 percent respectively, as rising prices and component shortages squeezed the market. Don't expect things to get better in the short term, as Counterpoint forecasts another 6 percent drop during 2027. But it believes that the market may see a 6 percent rebound in 2028, as memory supplies improve, pricing begins to stabilize, and pent-up demand for replacement phones returns. The 2026 outlook has been shaped by sharply rising component costs, particularly for DRAM and NAND flash. According to IDC , memory costs have risen approximately 350 percent since last year and are still climbing. As Reg readers will be well aware by now, this has been blamed on the memory manufacturers prioritizing output of high-margin chips to go into AI servers and GPU accelerators, creating a shortage of the mainstream components that are needed for devices like PCs and phones. Vendors have responded by raising prices, reducing memory configurations, and withdrawing lower-cost models. As The Register previously reported , memory costs accounted for almost 60 percent of the total bill of materials in sub-$400 smartphones during Q1 of 2026. For 2027, Counterpoint warns the outlook is for continued tight mobile DRAM supply, further price increases for low-power DDR (LPDDR) memory, and limited evidence to suggest short-term capacity increases. "The 2026 decline was initially expected to mark the low point of the cycle, but the memory situation has remained more restrictive than anticipated," said principal analyst Yang Wang. "Mobile memory allocation is still being displaced by AI and server demand, while higher costs are taking longer to move through handset portfolios and retail channels. The result is a much weaker 2027, particularly for lower priced devices and price sensitive markets." Global shipments are forecast to rebound by 6 percent in 2028, but that would bring shipments only roughly back to this year's already shrunken level, rather than hitting the peak of previous years. Counterpoint cautions that the scale of the rebound will depend on how quickly lower component costs translate into retail pricing. A speedy improvement in mobile memory allocation during the second half of 2027 could bring replacement demand forward and swell shipments, but continued competition from the AI market or another round of handset price increases would hinder recovery. technology.title: Bill for Birmingham's Oracle debacle reaches £128M
technology.description: Birmingham City Council faces a £128.1 million bill for its disastrous transition from SAP to Oracle – more than six times the original estimate for a project that contributed to its financial collapse. Papers presented to its Audit Committee this week put the combined cost of the original implementation, which went live in 2022, and this year's reimplementation at £128.1 million, against £19.96 million forecast in the 2019 business case [PDF]. The report , from program director Philip Macpherson, said the project's funding allocation had previously reached £157 million. The report said the new Oracle Fusion system went live in August without any priority-one or "showstopper" issues. "The program has now moved into the Post Go Live Support phase where [it] continues to provide extra support but slowly transitions towards 'Business As Usual' operating procedures," the report said. It is an understatement to say the same was not true of the first attempt to move the council's finance, HR, and payroll systems off its legacy R/3 SAP system to more modern software. The first project started in 2019 and was supposed to go live in April 2021, but was delayed by a year. After the council started to use the system in April 2022, it soon became beset by a series of serious problems. Although the council had planned to implement Oracle "out-of-the-box," it created several customizations, including a bank reconciliation system that failed to function properly. The council struggled to understand its cash position and was unable to produce auditable accounts . It has spent more than £5 million on manual workaround labor . The system move also contributed to it becoming effectively bankrupt , an event it failed to foresee due to the malfunctioning finance system. It later emerged that officials ignored a "red" warning prior to the go-live date. They were explicitly told the system could cause late payments, a failure to collect debt, and incorrect accounting if it went live. Officials gave the go-ahead regardless. The council decided to reimplement Oracle from scratch, while running the current system as best it could and implementing off-the-shelf software CivicaPay , now rebranded as Civica Income Management. Despite the apparently trouble-free relaunch, the true cost to the council is likely higher than the projected £128.1 million implementation bill. For a start, the original £19 million budget was supposed to support the software implementation for schools , but that was excluded from the reimplementation. Secondly, the council expected significant savings from moving to Oracle in 2022 through greater efficiency. The 2019 business case booked £27 million in savings from 2019 to 2031, for example. A 2024 analysis by Audit Reform Lab, based at the University of Sheffield, estimated that the disaster's direct and indirect financial impact, including lost savings and deteriorating tax collection, would reach £216.5 million by April 2026. technology.title: UK government rejects national consultation on AI datacenters
technology.description: The UK government has rejected calls for a UK-wide public consultation on the environmental impacts of AI datacenters, despite a petition attracting more than 39,000 signatures. Campaign group Protect the Wild launched the petition last month, calling for a national consultation that would consider whether further expansion should be restricted, paused, or halted until those impacts are properly understood and addressed. The nonprofit says the petition smashed the 10,000 signature threshold above which a government response is required in just three days, and the total stood at over 39,000 as this article was being prepared. In its response, published on November 23, the government ruled out the requested UK-wide environmental consultation, saying individual projects' impacts should be addressed through the planning process. It pointed instead to a separate consultation on its draft datacenter planning policy, open until January 8, 2027. "Datacenters are vital to the UK's digital economy. They underpin the digital services that people rely on every day, including public services, healthcare and the way people work. They also provide the infrastructure needed to develop and use AI," the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) says. "Building more capacity in the UK will support economic growth and innovation, while strengthening national resilience and ensuring the UK is well placed to realize the opportunities presented by AI." But it adds that the government recognizes the environmental impacts of bit barns are real and must be understood and mitigated, and this is one of the reasons why it established the Data Centre Covenant tests. This Covenant, published last month, sets out tests all compute sheds "are encouraged to meet," while "strategic datacenters" are required to meet them to qualify for additional government assistance. The government has yet to define which datacenters qualify as "strategic," saying it will publish further details and eligibility criteria in due course. Qualifying projects could receive help securing power and accelerating planning. Briefly, the Covenant tests are that operators cover any energy costs they create, so that communities do not have to pick up the bill; that they invest in local communities; adhere to the highest environmental standards; create jobs and drive reindustrialization; and provide secure and reliable access to their compute resources. If this has a ring of familiarity, it is because President Trump earlier this year introduced a Ratepayer Protection Pledge , under which hyperscalers and AI companies agreed to protect US consumers from any bill shocks due to the energy and infrastructure requirements of their datacenter projects. It seems that where the US leads, the UK still often follows. science.title: Dropping missiles from orbit? 2 European companies sign agreement to study the idea
science.description:
Julian Dossett is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He primarily covers the rocket industry and space exploration and, in addition to science writing, contributes travel stories to New Mexico Magazine. In 2022 and 2024, his travel writing earned IRMA Awards. Previously, he worked as a staff writer at CNET. He graduated from Texas State University in San Marcos in 2011 with a B.A. in philosophy. He owns a large collection of sci-fi pulp magazines from the 1960s.

A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit. Atmos, a space company known for its Phoenix reusable reentry vehicle , will work with MBDA, Europe's largest missile manufacturer, on the new project. "We are assessing how proven defense systems and new orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, said in a statement on Nov. 18. The system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies said that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration. Atmos and MBDA also said this work could lead to demonstrations, but the companies' announcement makes it clear that any deployment or use would be subject to the approval of governmental and military authorities. "The initiative also directly supports MBDA's broader strategic vision in the space domain, reinforcing both space for defense and the defense of space," Thomas Gottschild, MBDA Deutschland managing director, said in the same statement. This news comes a few months after Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said that the U.S. Space Force operates orbital weapons . "Let me be crystal clear: Today, Guardians operate on-orbit weapons that can defend the joint force against space-enabled attacks," Schiess said during a conferenace presentation on Sept. 15 ("Guardians" refers to Space Force personnel.) Last year, Atmos' Phoenix capsule got its first test run in space. The cargo-return technology launched aboard a Space X Falcon 9 rocket during a rideshare mission in February 2025. Atmos tested out the inflatable heat shields it has been working on to help future space-manufactured cargo make it through Earth's atmosphere in one piece. "Orbital transportation and return form a new layer of strategic infrastructure, and infrastructure determines what Europe can achieve on its own terms," Klaus said in the Nov 18 statement.

science.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
science.description: null Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W. It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination. But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone. The five stars are still there, but the shape you may have memorized looks like it's been picked up and turned over. It looks more like an E or an M, depending on when you look. Now try and look for the Big Dipper /the Plough. It's gone. Nothing mysterious has happened, of course. Cassiopeia is doing exactly what it always does, but it's a reminder that the northern sky is where you can easily watch the stars move — and the seasons turn. What's happening and when to look Stars move anti-clockwise around the north celestial pole, so Cassiopeia changes orientation. (Image credit: Alan Dyer/Stocktrek Images via Getty Images) Late November is an excellent time to reacquaint yourself with Cassiopeia from anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere. Look high in the northern sky during the evening for its five prominent stars — Caph, Schedar, Navi, Ruchbah and Segin. Depending on exactly when you look, it can look like a W, E, M or a 3. This is because Cassiopeia is circumpolar. Rather than rising in the east and eventually setting in the west like many familiar constellations , it circles the north celestial pole — a position currently held by Polaris , the North Star. From sufficiently northerly latitudes, its main stars never disappear below the horizon. This gives us a simple observing experiment. Find Cassiopeia in the early evening and remember its orientation relative to the horizon. Go back several hours later and look again. The constellation has moved around Polaris, and its shape has changed. The stars haven't changed their arrangement — Earth has simply rotated from west to east. We all know this logically, but watching the familiar pattern of Cassiopeia's stars apparently tip over during a single night makes Earth's rotation a lot less abstract. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 27, 1885: Astronomer captures 1st known photo of a meteor during an Andromedid meteor storm
science.description: null On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. The picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek. He captured the trail of the meteor on a photographic plate in the Czech Republic. The meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower . The Andromedids were associated with Biela's Comet , which broke apart in the 1850s. When Weinek observed the meteor shower in 1885, it was in the middle of a meteor storm . This means that there were way more meteors than usual. Skywatchers could see thousands of meteors per hour. The November 1872 incidence of the Andromedid meteor shower, as seen over France, in a painting. (Image credit: Alto Vintage Images/Alamy) Why it mattered Not many stargazers may be be acquainted with the Andromedid meteor shower. What used to be a spectacular annual meteor shower is now hardly even visible. But in 1885, the Andromedids were an annual treat for skywatchers hoping for a chance to see the remains of Biela's comet (a comet first spotted in 1772 and then found - for the third time - in 1826 by the German astronomer Wilhelm von Biela, from whom it gets its name). Meteor Shower Quiz: How Well Do You Know 'Shooting Stars'? This modern photo of the Geminid meteor shower shows dozens of meteors captured in a long exposure by Josh Drury. Ladislaus Weinek, who captured the first photo of a meteor, had to use a photographic plate in 1889. (Image credit: Josh Dury) Camera technology has come a long way since 1885, which is good since it is a bit harder to see the Andromedids these days. Instead of photographic plates or digital cameras, astronomers now have to use special tracking equipment to record images of Andromedid meteors. In 2011, astronomers announced that the meteor shower seemed to be undergoing a resurgence of activity, with 50 meteors per hour, and upticks were expected in 2018 and 2023. Want more space history? science.title: Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'
science.description: null Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star. That isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao. A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER). "The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events." Reconstructing a violent cosmic collision The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy , a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion. Responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years, They determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits. "A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar said. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years." science.description: A detail from Joseph Wright’s 1771 painting The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, showing Henning Brand in 1669 Science History Images/Alamy Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history. Of course, science doesn’t work that way; even if breakthroughs shift the paradigm of our understanding, discovery doesn’t progress like a tech tree in a computer game, but as an interweaving tapestry of complementary and competing ideas and experimentation. Theories can bubble under the surface for centuries, overlooked because of politics or failure to realise their implications, while innovations can emerge from taking an idea in one industry and transplanting it to another. But, for a moment, try and picture what just one such ingredient could be. What would you pick? For centuries, in medieval Europe, alchemists quested for the “Philosopher’s Stone” that would finally help them achieve their dreams of transmutation. It was a search doomed to failure from the very beginning. And yet, a far better idea was under their noses – or, rather, their underpants – the entire time. My pick? Urine has a strong case for being the most transformative substance in human history. It required the first chemical reaction we mastered – fire – to keep us warm, cook our food and smelt ores. But leatherwork played an equally key role. Urine is a source of urea, which bacteria can break down into ammonia, granting early humans easy access to a base that could soften organic matter and tan hides. Across the world, leatherwork became the cornerstone of survival for every civilisation, from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia: even cultures that didn’t develop a bronze age, such as the Aztec, or skipped it entirely, as seen in Sub-Saharan Africa, relied on leatherwork for clothes, structures, industry and commerce. When the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on November 8, 2026, clouds encroached on the snowy mountain on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula . But they hovered beneath the volcano’s 3,283-meter (10,771-foot) peak, leaving a clear opening over its caldera and northern upper slopes. The upper reaches of Shivelyuch feature a caldera 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) wide that is open to the south. A lava dome , formed by vents extruding viscous magma, appears as a dark area within it. Lava domes on Shivelyuch go through cycles of growth and collapse, with collapses sometimes setting off fast-moving avalanches of hot ash and rock called pyroclastic flows . In November 2026, effusive eruptions of lava and explosive activity at Shivelyuch had been ongoing for months , according to reports from the Kamchatka Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT). And despite frequent cloudiness, satellites regularly detect thermal anomalies from the volcano. On the day of this image, KVERT reported that a plume of resuspended ash drifted 120 kilometers (75 miles) to the east. That kind of activity is relatively tame for the mountain. Explosions from Shivelyuch periodically send ash several kilometers up into the atmosphere, where it can travel great distances and pose risks to aircraft . In July 2026, an ash plume rode the jet stream over the Bering Sea into Alaskan airspace, according to news reports , prompting the cancellation of multiple flights. science.title: Venus shines at its brightest in the predawn sky this week. Here's where to look
science.description: null Venus is at its most dazzling in the predawn sky this week as it shines close to the bright star Spica in the southeast. Here's what you need to know. As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky. Instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances. All the while, its shifting moon-like phases and ever-changing proximity to Earth causes its brightness to wax and wane. When is Venus at its most dazzling? Venus will reach peak brightness during its current morning apparition at 1:37 p.m. EST (1837 GMT) on Nov. 27 according to the astronomy website In-The-Sky . Stargazers in the U.S. could get an incredible view of Venus in the predawn hours of the coming week, as the planet climbs into the southeastern sky ahead of the rising sun, with Mercury clinging close to the horizon below. Celestron Nexstar 4SE (Image credit: Celestron) This is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. For a closer look at craters and the terminator, make sure to grab a 9mm or 12mm eyepiece and get stronger magnification. _ Celestron Nexstar 4SE review The bright star Spica will glow less than five degrees away from Venus before dawn on Nov. 27 — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length against the night sky. Spica is a double system of two stars that orbit one another once every four days. Its stars are separated by just approximately 11 million miles (less than 18 million kilometers), making them far too close to split visually with even the most powerful amateur equipment. However, the system still makes for a dazzling target, appearing as a magnificent blue-white star when viewed through the eyepiece of a 4-inch telescope. Venus will appear close to Spica in the southeastern sky. (Image credit: Starry Night Pro 8) Check that the sun is safely below the horizon before turning your telescope on Venus to observe a crescent of light playing across the planet's dense atmosphere. Over the coming weeks and months, Venus will appear increasingly illuminated as it moves farther away from Earth in its orbit, while its apparent size through a telescope will gradually decrease. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 26, 2011: NASA's 2-ton nuclear-powered Curiosity rover launches to Mars
science.description: null On November 26, 2011, the NASA Curiosity rover launched to Mars. The Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet. The 2-ton science laboratory is about the size of a small SUV. The mission's goal was to search for habitable environments on Mars , or evidence that the planet could have been habitable in the past. It launched on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. About nine months later, Curiosity made a challenging landing on Mars. It successfully used a new landing technology called a sky crane to gently lower it to the surface. NASA's Curiosity rover lifts off atop a United Launch Alliance Atlas V rocket on Nov. 26, 2011 from Florida's Cape Canaveral Air Force Station. (Image credit: collectSPACE/Robert Z. Pearlman ) Why it mattered It may be hard to imagine now, but 15 years ago, the idea of a nuclear-powered rover on Mars was just a concept. When the Curiosity rover launched in 2011, it made that idea a reality the car-size probe (using a plutonium-based radioisotope thermoelectric generator that converts heat from radioactive decay into power) as it headed to the Red Planet. Curiosity was the largest rover ever launched to Mars, following up on the success of the tiny Sojourner rover in 1997 and the larger twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity in 2004. Its sky crane landing system was novel at the time, and fully automated. Once it began its descent in August 2012, NASA could only wait through "seven minutes of terror" to see how it turned out. It ended being a huge success. NASA's Curiosity rover on Mars. (Image credit: NASA) After its smooth landing, Curiosity lived up to its original name: the Mars Science Laboratory. Within weeks, Curiosity fulfilled its primary mission. It found evidence of ancient running water on Mars . It later found organic molecules on Mars as well. Curiosity's primary mission was expected to last just about one Martian year (687 Earth days, or about two Earth years), as the rover explored its Gale Crater landing site. But NASA has extended the mission as the rover continues to operate in good health. In fact, Curiosity has survived long enough to welcome its successor to Mars, the Perseverance rover , which landed in February 2021 on a mission to collect the first samples for later retrieval. Perseverance used the same basic 2-ton design, plutonium power system and sky crane landing system to reach Mars. And today, a ground-based twin of the Curiosity rover, called Promise , is being outfitted for an upcoming mission to the moon. Want more space history?
